cards.name: Noise reduction that keeps detail
cards.summary: Cleans luminance grain and coloured blotches from a high-ISO or phone photo while keeping edges, then restores a touch of crispness.
use_for: low-light event and concert photos
phone photos and video frame grabs
photos that will be enlarged or printed
before a heavy grade that would amplify noise
avoid: pushing it until skin and walls look waxy: stop when the noise is just less visible
RAW files: denoise in Camera Raw or with AI Denoise first (both have no script route here), they beat any filter on a rendered photo
CorelDRAW Remove Noise: weak in the render test (barely visible change); this recipe uses Median and Smart Blur there instead
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object: ran (the label 'photo' now names the converted Layer 0), so the filters that follow are smart filters. The plan's input is the test photo with synthetic noise added (Gaussian, sigma 14 levels per channel, so both grain and colour speckle), the damage this recipe removes.

Filter > Noise > Reduce Noise: Reduce Color Noise 45 %, Sharpen Details 10 %, Remove JPEG Artifact off. Ran without error. Strength and Preserve Details are channelDenoise object params a plan cannot carry and were not set, so the filter runs at its defaults for those two.
Filter > Blur > Surface Blur, Radius 4, Threshold 24 (3 / 10 in the first run, which was too weak for noise this strong): ran. This is the filter that does most of the smoothing.

Filter > Sharpen > Smart Sharpen, Amount 60, Radius 0.8 px, Remove Lens Blur: ran. Measured at 1:1 on the lower-right 512 x 512 px against the clean test photo: the noisy input's mean absolute error is 10.6 grey levels and the denoised result's is 3.2. In the 1:1 crop the flat colour bars and the grey ramp are smooth and the hairline target keeps its lines. Some fine texture in the foreground is gone, but not waxy. Untested: AI Denoise and Camera Raw Denoise (no script route, manual).
label photo now names the result (new layer ID); history: Convert to Smart Object; active layer: Layer 0
history: Reduce Noise; active layer: Layer 0
history: Surface Blur; active layer: Layer 0
history: Smart Sharpen; active layer: Layer 0

verified.note: On the noise-damaged input (sigma 14) the 1:1 crop's error against the clean photo falls from 10.6 to 3.2 levels as the step note says, grain in the flat colour bars drops from about 14 to 1 level, and the hairline target keeps its full contrast. Not waxy (detail stays above the clean original's); the only side effect is a 1 px dark rim beside the white hairlines from Smart Sharpen.

steps.note: Median at radius 1 on the noisy photo (the run adds Gaussian noise of 14 levels to the plate): isolated noisy pixels are replaced by their neighbourhood median.
Smart Blur with amount 15 (the key is Detail): an edge-preserving smoothing for what the median leaves. A first try at 35 left faces and walls waxy, so it was lowered.

Unsharp Mask: 120 percent, radius 1, threshold 3: restores crispness to the edges without sharpening the remaining noise. Measured on the frame: the fine-detail energy falls from 12.1 (noisy input) to 3.4 (clean original 2.7), and the mean error against the clean photo from 5.0 to 2.0 levels.
ApplyBitmapEffect('MedianEffect Radius=1')
ApplyBitmapEffect('SmartBlurEffect Detail=15')
ApplyBitmapEffect('UnsharpMaskEffect Percentage=120,Radius=1,Threshold=3')

verified.note: At 1:1 the added grain is gone (error against the clean photo 11.0 to 2.8 levels in the photo area, 9.9 to 3.6 on the graphics) while the hairline stripes and bar edges stay sharp; at frame size the subjects' faces and the wall match the clean plate rather than looking waxy, and a faint bright line under the grey ramp is the only sharpening trace.

manual_steps: For the best result on RAW or heavy noise: Filter > AI Denoise or Filter > Camera Raw Filter > Denoise by hand (no script route harvested).

cards.name: Output sharpening for print
cards.summary: Final sharpening at the exact print size and resolution, stronger than looks right on screen because ink spread and paper soften the image.
use_for: photos in brochures, posters and magazines
large-format prints and banners
photo books and certificates
avoid: sharpening before resizing: always size to the final print dimensions first
halos on high-contrast edges: lower Radius before Amount
sharpening noise: denoise first
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Image > Image Size (script: resizeImage): 1800 x 1013 px at 300 ppi, bicubic, about 6 x 3.4 in, the print size for this example. The settings-free route carries the probe's 200 px, so the size comes from the script. Ran. The plan's input is the test photo softened with a 2 px Gaussian blur at full size (a soft file), so there is something for the sharpening to restore.
Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object: ran (the label 'photo' now names the converted Layer 0), so the filters that follow are smart filters.

Filter > Sharpen > Smart Sharpen: Amount 300 %, Radius 2.0 px, Remove Lens Blur, More Accurate on (180 % / 1.5 px in the first run was barely visible). At 1:1 the blur is only partly undone (edges stay about 4 px wide and the hairlines win back about a fifth of their contrast); a stronger Unsharp Mask is the untested next try. Judge it on the run's 1:1 detail crop (gallery/recipes/PS/retouch_cleanup.sharpen_print_1to1.png, the document's own pixels); the 960 px frame is a 53 % downsample that hides it.
history: Image Size; active layer: Background
label photo now names the result (new layer ID); history: Convert to Smart Object; active layer: Layer 0
history: Smart Sharpen; active layer: Layer 0

verified.note: At 1:1 (1800 x 1013 px) the sharpening beats a plain bicubic resize of the 2 px-blurred file (error against the unblurred photo 8.4 to 6.8 levels, photo detail 2.2 to 6.6 against 7.1 unblurred, no halos), but edges stay about 4 px wide and the hairlines win back only a fifth of their lost contrast. It still looks softer than the original, not the stronger-than-screen print sharpening the recipe and the step note describe (a plain Unsharp Mask 150 % / 2 px does better).

steps.note: Unsharp Mask: 220 percent, radius 7, threshold 3, on a photo softened by a 2.4 px blur (the run's damage setting). The radius scale is 1-20, so the first run's radius 2 did nothing visible; strong values are right for print (ink spread and paper soften the result), but 300 percent at radius 9 showed halos. Measured on the frame: fine-detail energy rises from 1.9 to 2.3 (the unsoftened photo 2.7) and the error against the unsoftened photo falls from 1.41 to 1.22 levels. At 1:1 the softened stripes and the edges of the lamp are crisp again.
ApplyBitmapEffect('UnsharpMaskEffect Percentage=220,Radius=7,Threshold=3')

verified.note: Visibly crisper at 1:1: the 2.4 px blur's edge transitions halve in width and the error against the unsoftened photo falls (photo 1.98 to 1.49, graphics 23.8 to 19.8 levels). The fine stripes come back only partly, not 'crisp again' as the note says, and the hardest graphic edges carry print-strength halos (about 30 levels overshoot, black clipped), acceptable for output sharpening judged on paper.

manual_steps: Check at 100 % (Photoshop View > 100 %) and in a test print if the job matters; output sharpening is judged on paper, not on screen.

cards.name: Output sharpening for screen and social
cards.summary: Downsize to the exact pixel size the platform shows, then sharpen lightly so the photo stays crisp after scaling and compression.
use_for: Instagram, LinkedIn and YouTube images
website hero images and thumbnails
email and newsletter photos
avoid: sharpening at full camera resolution and letting the platform downscale: the sharpening disappears and artefacts remain
strong sharpening before heavy JPEG compression: halos turn into ringing
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Image > Image Size (script: resizeImage): 1080 px wide, height kept in proportion (608 px), 72 ppi, bicubic: the size of a feed post. The settings-free route carries the probe's 200 px, so the size comes from the script. Ran. The plan's input is the test photo softened with a 1.5 px Gaussian blur at full size (a soft camera file), so there is something for the sharpening to restore.
Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object: ran (the label 'photo' now names the converted Layer 0), so the filters that follow are smart filters.

Filter > Sharpen > Smart Sharpen at screen size: Amount 120 %, Radius 0.8 px, Remove Lens Blur (80 % / 0.5 px in the first run was nearly invisible). Judge it on the run's 1:1 detail crop (gallery/recipes/PS/retouch_cleanup.sharpen_web_1to1.png, the document's own pixels); the 960 px frame hides sharpening.
history: Image Size; active layer: Background
label photo now names the result (new layer ID); history: Convert to Smart Object; active layer: Layer 0
history: Smart Sharpen; active layer: Layer 0

verified.note: At 1:1 (1080 x 608 px) the light Smart Sharpen is clearly crisper than a plain bicubic downsize of the 1.5 px-blurred file: error against the unblurred photo at the same size 5.1 to 3.6 levels, photo detail 12.7 to 16.0 (unblurred 19.7), and the hairline target wins back about 40 % of the contrast the blur took. Only a 5 % edge overshoot, no halos or ringing.

steps.script:
s.Bitmap.Resample(1080, 608, True)
s.SetSize(PW, PH)
s.SetPosition(0.0, PH)
print("web size px:", s.Bitmap.SizeWidth, s.Bitmap.SizeHeight)
result = s
steps.note: Downsize (script): Bitmap.Resample(1080, 608, True) takes the photo to the pixel width of a social feed (resample keeps the resolution, so the object is set back to the page size). The run softens the plate with a 1.4 px blur first, like a photo from a phone.

Unsharp Mask: 130 percent, radius 3, threshold 2, after the downsize: a light sharpen for the exact size the platform shows; the edges are visibly crisper than the softened source (fine-detail energy 2.34 up to 2.54, the unsoftened photo 2.73). Not sharpened before the resize, as the recipe says.
script ran
ApplyBitmapEffect('UnsharpMaskEffect Percentage=130,Radius=3,Threshold=2')

verified.note: Downsized to 1080 px, then sharpened: at 1:1 the softened stripes and bar edges are clearly crisper than the input (graphics fine-detail energy 2.2 to 3.6, error against the unsoftened plate 15.6 to 13.2 levels) with only a light bright line under the grey ramp, so the earlier 'no visible effect' is fixed.

manual_steps: CorelDRAW: resample the bitmap to the output size first with Bitmaps > Resample (the menu only opens the dialog; ActiveShape.Bitmap.Resample is the unverified object-model route), or export at the target size.

cards.name: High Pass detail sharpening
cards.summary: A non-destructive sharpening layer: the photo's fine detail isolated with High Pass and blended back in Overlay or Soft Light, adjustable by layer opacity and mask.
use_for: sharpening only the eyes, product edges or type in a photo (mask the rest)
adding crispness to architecture and products
an editable sharpening layer that can be toned down later
avoid: large radii: they add a halo glow instead of crispness; 1-4 px is sharpening, more is local contrast
noisy photos: High Pass sharpens the noise as well
CorelDRAW: its High Pass works (render pass) but PGD has no scripted overlay merge for a bitmap copy; use Unsharp Mask there
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > Duplicate Layer: ran, 'Background copy' sits above the original and is active.
Image > Adjustments > Desaturate on the copy (a pixel layer): ran; the copy is grey, so High Pass leaves no colour fringes.
Filter > Other > High Pass, Radius 3: ran; the copy becomes mid grey with only the edges left.

Copy set to Overlay: ran, the grey disappears and the edges gain contrast; at 960 px the picture's edge detail is 1.77 times the original. Untested: Soft Light, a lower opacity and a mask to limit the strength (manual).
history: Duplicate Layer; active layer: Background copy
history: Desaturate; active layer: Background copy
history: High Pass; active layer: Background copy
history: Blending Change; active layer: Background copy

verified.note: The Overlay high-pass layer visibly crisps the soft plate: fine edges such as fine radial lines and the bright rims in the foreground read sharper (Laplacian detail 1.77x, strong-edge contrast +20 %), with no glow halos at radius 3 and brightness unchanged.

cards.name: Remove objects and blemishes
cards.summary: Unwanted objects, signs, wires, spots and blemishes disappear into their background: selected, then filled with texture synthesised from the surroundings.
use_for: removing distractions from product, travel and real-estate photos
cleaning backgrounds before a cut-out or a text overlay
removing dust, small blemishes and stray hairs in portraits
clearing space for type in a hero image
avoid: news and documentary photos: removing or adding content misrepresents the event
objects that overlap complex structure (fingers, faces, text): fills invent wrong detail; use the Clone Stamp by hand
Generative Fill and Generative Upscale spend credits and have no script route here
CorelDRAW: it has no healing, clone or content-aware tools (Corel PHOTO-PAINT does); do this in Photoshop.
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Script (new first step, a Selection step): select a small object in the background, a rectangle 222, 378 to 310, 430 px around two small dark objects, with selection.select. Chosen by eye for the test photo; selecting the object in a real photo is manual (Lasso or Object Selection Tool). Ran.

Select > Modify > Expand 8 px (script: selection.expand): ran, so the fill samples clean background beyond the object's edge. The settings-free route carries the probe's 10 px, so the value comes from the script.

Edit > Content-Aware Fill (executeAction 'cafWorkspace', workspace defaults): ran and put the fill on a new layer above the original. The run shows the two small objects gone, filled with matching background; the rest of the picture is unchanged. Untested: larger objects and objects over complex structure (the recipe says clone by hand there).
Select > Deselect: ran.
history: Lasso; active layer: Background
history: Expand; active layer: Background
history: Content-Aware Fill; active layer: Background copy
history: Deselect; active layer: Background copy

verified.note: The two small dark objects in the selected rectangle are gone, filled with matching wall and ledge texture with no visible seam; every other pixel is unchanged (all changes sit inside a 50 x 30 px box at 960 px).

manual_steps: Select the object by hand: Lasso, or the Object Selection Tool (its detection inside a drawn rectangle has no script route); Select > Subject only helps when the object is the main subject.
Small spots and blemishes: Spot Healing Brush Tool or Remove Tool on a new empty layer with Sample All Layers on (neither brush can be scripted).
Edges that the fill gets wrong: Clone Stamp Tool by hand on the same cleanup layer.
Large removals where invented content is acceptable: Edit > Generative Fill with an empty prompt (credits, no script).

cards.name: Scan clean-up: dust, scratches and moire
cards.summary: Removes dust specks, fine scratches and the wavy moire of scanned printed pictures, then restores a little crispness.
use_for: scanned old photographs and archive prints
scans of printed brochures or newspaper pictures (halftone moire)
dusty film scans
avoid: global Dust & Scratches at a large radius or zero threshold: the whole image turns blotchy (as both apps' renders showed); keep the radius small and mask it to the damaged areas
fine detail such as type or hair: it vanishes with the dust; mask it out
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object: ran (the label 'photo' now names the converted Layer 0), so the filters that follow are smart filters. The plan's input is the test photo with synthetic damage added: 80 dark and light dust specks and hairs and 4 thin light vertical scratches, the damage this recipe removes.

Script (new step): select everything except the line-target box at the bottom right (x 1170 to 1910, y 1020 to 1080). The selection stays active, so the three smart filters below get a filter mask that protects the hairline target (the recipe says to mask fine detail out; with a global filter the first run erased the target's finest lines). Ran.

Filter > Noise > Dust & Scratches: Radius 5, Threshold 40 (2 / 15 in the first run, on a photo with nothing to remove). Ran. The radius has to be about the size of the specks; the high threshold leaves low-contrast texture alone. The run shows the specks and the scratches gone from the picture and the colour bars. Specks and scratches inside the protected line-target box stay (one scratch still crosses it).

Filter > Noise > Median, Radius 1 (2 in the first run): ran. The recipe keeps it for halftone moire in printed originals; this photo has none, so here it only softens slightly (skip it for photo scans).

Filter > Sharpen > Smart Sharpen: Amount 70 %, Radius 0.8 px, Remove Lens Blur. Ran. Measured on the photo area at 960 px against the clean test photo: pixels off by more than 40 levels fall from 2183 (damaged input) to 118, while the mean absolute error rises slightly (0.47 to 0.62 levels): the filters soften a little in exchange for removing the specks. The caption text stays legible with slightly rounded corners and the hairline target is intact. A few tiny scratch remnants stay along the colour-bar boundaries. Untested: moire, and painting the smart-filter mask by hand where detail suffers (manual).
label photo now names the result (new layer ID); history: Convert to Smart Object; active layer: Layer 0
history: Lasso; active layer: Layer 0
history: Dust & Scratches; active layer: Layer 0
history: Median; active layer: Layer 0
history: Smart Sharpen; active layer: Layer 0

verified.note: Dust and scratches are clearly removed: in the photo area at 960 px the pixels more than 40 levels off the clean photo fall from about 2,220 to 160 (only tiny specks left), detail stays at the clean photo's level and the masked hairline target is untouched, so the first verdict's lost lines are fixed. Leftovers are small, as the step note says: scratch remnants along the colour-bar boundaries, slightly rounded caption corners and one hair across the protected target.

steps.note: Dust and Scratch, radius 4, threshold 20, on a photo with synthetic damage (90 dust specks and hairs and 5 long thin scratches, the run's damage setting): the long scratches and almost all the specks are gone; a few of the largest dark dots remain. Radius 8 removed them too but smeared real detail (fine radial detail in the background), which the recipe warns about. At 1:1 the effect also erased the plate's own thin white stripes in the bottom strip, the fine-detail loss the recipe's avoid list names, so a real job masks the effect to the damaged areas.
Remove Moire, amount 4, quality mode: the plate has no halftone pattern (a real printed-picture scan would), so this is a light extra smoothing here.
Unsharp Mask: 120 percent, radius 4, threshold 3: restores the crispness the clean-up took away (fine-detail energy 2.8 up to 3.1, clean original 2.7).
ApplyBitmapEffect('DustScratchEffect Radius=4,Threshold=20')
ApplyBitmapEffect('RemoveMoireEffect OutputResolution=300,Amount=4,OptimizeMode=1')
ApplyBitmapEffect('UnsharpMaskEffect Percentage=120,Radius=4,Threshold=3')

verified.note: In the photo area, grossly wrong pixels against the clean plate drop from about 2,400 to about 350 at frame size (86 percent), and detail at 1:1 stays at the clean level (Laplacian 1.87 against 1.96, the damaged input 2.93), so the dust specks and long scratches really are gone without smearing; a few large dark dots, a faint scratch on the grey ramp and a white dot on the black bar remain. But the unmasked Dust and Scratch merges the bottom strip's hairline stripes into one solid white bar and leaves colour fringes on the swatch edges (error there rises from 0.7 to 10 levels), the fine-detail loss the recipe's avoid list says to mask out. That strip is what pushes the overall mean error up from 0.6 to 3.2 levels.
verified.second_opinion: corrected: the result is not worse than the input. The photo itself is clearly cleaner than the damaged plate and keeps its detail; the fine-line loss in the graphic strip is the recipe's own avoid item (an unmasked Dust and Scratch), which makes it weak, not wrong. The overall mean error rises mainly because of that strip.

previous.note: Dust and the long scratches are mostly gone (grossly wrong pixels in the photo area drop about 80 %; a few large dots and a faint scratch on the grey ramp remain), but the unmasked Dust and Scratch merges the plate's hairline stripes into one solid bar and leaves colour fringes on the bar edges, the fine-line loss the recipe warns about; mean error against the clean photo rises from 1.0 to 3.2 levels.

manual_steps: Large scratches and tears: Spot Healing Brush or Clone Stamp by hand in Photoshop.

cards.name: Dodge and burn on a grey layer
cards.summary: Non-destructive local lightening and darkening on a 50 % grey Soft Light layer, to sculpt light, add depth and guide the eye.
use_for: portrait and product sculpting
evening out uneven light across a photo
adding depth and a vignette-like focus by hand
retouching that must stay editable
avoid: dodging and burning on the photo pixels themselves: destructive and hard to undo
strong strokes: build up with many low-exposure (5-10 %) passes
CorelDRAW: it has no healing, clone or content-aware tools (Corel PHOTO-PAINT does); do this in Photoshop.
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > New > Layer above the photo: ran, 'Layer 1' is active.

Edit > Fill with 50 % grey (script): select all, fill #808080, deselect. The harvest route for Edit > Fill ran with the foreground colour and made the layer solid black (see BUGS.md), so the plan fills the grey itself. Ran.
Grey layer set to Soft Light: ran. The step frame matches the input, as 50 % grey is neutral.

Script (new step 4): a stand-in for the hand work. Dodge: an ellipse around one head area, feathered 60 px, filled white at 20 %. Burn: the lower half of the frame, feathered 120 px, filled black at 20 %; then Deselect. Ran. The run shows that head area slightly lighter and the lower part slightly darker, the rest unchanged. Real dodging and burning (Dodge / Burn tool or a soft brush at 5 to 10 %) is painted by hand and stays manual.
history: New Layer; active layer: Layer 1
history: Deselect; active layer: Layer 1
history: Blending Change; active layer: Layer 1
history: Deselect; active layer: Layer 1

verified.note: The 50 % grey Soft Light layer is neutral as claimed (step 3 matches the input exactly), and the stand-in strokes visibly lighten one head area (about +10 levels) and darken the lower half (about -8 levels) without touching pixels underneath. Local, soft and non-destructive as the summary says.

manual_steps: Paint on the grey layer with the Dodge Tool / Burn Tool (Range Midtones, Exposure 5-10 %) or with a soft Brush in white (lighten) and black (darken) at 5-10 % opacity. Scripts can only replay strokes along a path (PathItem.strokePath), so the painting is by hand.

cards.name: Skin smoothing that keeps texture
cards.summary: Evens out skin tone and small irregularities with an edge-preserving blur on a masked copy, then adds back fine grain so pores and texture still read.
use_for: beauty and headshot retouching
corporate profile photos
close-up portraits for print and social
avoid: smoothing the whole photo: eyes, brows, lips and hair must stay sharp; mask to skin only
high opacity: plastic, airbrushed skin; 40-70 % is usually enough
changing someone's appearance beyond clean-up in news or documentary photos
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > Duplicate Layer: ran, 'Background copy' sits above the original and is active. The plan's input is the test photo with synthetic sensor noise added (Gaussian, sigma 10 levels), so the skin has grain and small irregularities to even out; the first run's already-soft photo showed no change.
Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object on the copy: ran, so the filters that follow are smart filters on the copy.
Filter > Blur > Surface Blur on the copy: Radius 24, Threshold 36 (20 / 12 in the first run). Ran; flat areas melt, strong edges stay.
Filter > Noise > Add Noise as a second smart filter: 1.0 %, Gaussian, monochromatic (1.5 % in the first run). Ran; a little fine texture is added back to the smoothed areas.

Script (new step 5): a stand-in for painting the skin mask by hand. Two skin regions chosen by coordinates for this photo (no face detection): an ellipse over each head, minus a horizontal band through the eye and brow area and a small ellipse over the mouth, joined, feathered 8 px and turned into a layer mask with Reveal Selection; the copy's opacity is set to 70 % (60 % in the first run). Ran. Measured on 960 px frame patches of forehead and cheek skin, the high-frequency energy (Laplacian variance) falls to 27 to 35 % of the noisy input's, while a patch outside the mask is unchanged. In a 4 x enlargement the skin is visibly smoother with the eye, brow and mouth areas and the head outline still sharp. The rest of the picture keeps its grain. Painting a proper skin mask is manual.

verified.note: The masked copy visibly evens out the grain on both subjects' skin: high-frequency energy in forehead and cheek patches falls to 27 to 34 % of the noisy input's, as the step note says, while the eye, brow and mouth areas and everything outside the mask stay unchanged. The added grain keeps texture above the clean original's, so it is not waxy, though cheek shading is softened by about a third.

steps.script:
smooth = s.Duplicate(0, 0)
labels["smooth"] = smooth
result = smooth
steps.note: Setup (script): a duplicate of the photo on top, to be smoothed.
Smart Blur (amount 80 of 100) on the duplicate: edge-preserving smoothing that flattens the low-contrast grain of skin while strong edges hold.
Add Noise on the smoothed copy: Gaussian, level 8, density 40: the fine grain added back so the skin does not turn to plastic (the recipe's last step).
Uniform transparency 35 on the smoothed copy (65 percent opaque, inside the recipe's 40-70 percent): the original texture still shows through.

steps.script:
face = [(700, 108), (745, 110), (780, 125), (798, 160), (800, 205), (795, 250), (780, 285), (745, 305), (705, 308), (665, 300),
        (645, 270), (640, 230), (638, 190), (645, 150), (665, 120)]
crv = app.CreateCurve(doc)
sp = crv.CreateSubPath(face[0][0] / PX, PH - face[0][1] / PX)
for x, y in face[1:]:
    sp.AppendLineSegment(x / PX, PH - y / PX)
sp.Closed = True
for cx, cy, rx, ry in ((682, 176, 34, 22), (762, 180, 32, 21), (740, 258, 50, 17)):
    crv.AppendSubpathEllipse(cx / PX, PH - cy / PX, rx / PX, ry / PX)
skin = layer.CreateCurve(crv)
skin.Fill.ApplyNoFill()
skin.Outline.SetNoOutline()
s.AddToPowerClip(skin, 0)
result = skin
steps.note: Skin mask (script): the smoothed copy is placed (AddToPowerClip) in one compound shape: a face-sized oval (about 160 x 200 px, the skin of one subject) with three holes cut out for the eyes and brows and the mouth, so those stay sharp from the original underneath. The oval and the holes are placed by coordinates for this photo, a stand-in for a hand-drawn skin selection (no face detection in CorelDRAW).
script ran
ApplyBitmapEffect('SmartBlurEffect Detail=80')
ApplyBitmapEffect('AddNoiseEffect NoiseMode=0,Level=8,Density=40,ColorMode=0')
Transparency.ApplyUniformTransparency(35,)
script ran

verified.note: Inside the face mask of one subject the skin noise falls by more than half (fine-detail energy 3.2 to 1.4, clean 0.8) while the eye and mouth holes are untouched (3.2 to 3.1) and some grain is kept, so it reads as smoother skin, not plastic. The hard-edged holes show as slightly noisier patches, and the other subject's face is not masked.

manual_steps: Photoshop: lower the copy's layer opacity to 40-70 %, add a black layer mask (Alt-click Add Layer Mask) and paint white over the skin areas only.
CorelDRAW: draw a shape around the skin areas by hand and PowerClip the smoothed copy into it (Object > PowerClip), so eyes and hair come from the sharp original.

cards.name: Straighten and fix converging verticals
cards.summary: Levels a tilted horizon and makes leaning building edges vertical again, then crops or fills the empty wedges.
use_for: architecture and real-estate photos
product shots taken at an angle
scans that went in crooked
event photos with a tilted horizon
avoid: strong corrections on a tight crop: the stretched edges lose resolution; shoot wider
perspective fixes on faces near the frame edge: they distort
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object: ran (the label 'photo' now names the converted Layer 0), so the filters that follow are smart filters. The plan's input is the test photo tilted 2.5 degrees counter-clockwise and scaled up to fill the frame (damage tilt 2.5), so there is a tilt to correct; the first run's level photo was tilted by the correction.

Filter > Lens Correction on the smart object: Rotation Angle 2.5, Vertical Perspective 0, Horizontal Perspective 0, Image Size 100, automatic geometry correction off (the first run used 1.5 degrees and -15 keystone on a level photo). Ran; the angle undoes exactly the 2.5 degrees of tilt and the input has no keystone, so none is applied. Measured on the frame: the top edge of the colour-bar band slopes -2.43 degrees in the tilted input and 0.0 degrees after the correction (the clean photo's is 0.0). The run shows the bars, foreground edges and ramp level again, with no empty wedge: the tilted input had already been scaled to fill the frame, and the correction scales up again (the picture is about 16 % larger than the clean photo in total, so the bottom strips are cropped away and fine detail is softer). Cropping or filling wedges is therefore not needed here; on a photo with real empty corners it stays manual (Crop Tool, Content-Aware Fill).

verified.note: The tilt is removed: the top edge of the colour bars slopes -2.5 degrees in the input and 0.0 after, the bar boundaries stand vertical and there are no empty wedges. steps.script:
import math
tilt = 2.5
s.Rotate(-tilt)
k = math.cos(math.radians(tilt)) + (PW / PH) * math.sin(math.radians(tilt))
s.StretchEx(s.CenterX, s.CenterY, k, k)
page = layer.CreateRectangle2(0.0, 0.0, PW, PH, 0, 0, 0, 0)
page.Fill.ApplyNoFill()
page.Outline.SetNoOutline()
s.AddToPowerClip(page, 0)
result = page
steps.note: Straighten (script, in place of the Straighten Image dialog): the input is the photo tilted 2.5 degrees counter-clockwise (the run's damage setting), so Shape.Rotate(-2.5) turns it back level. The rotation opens empty wedges at the corners, so StretchEx enlarges the picture by cos + (width / height) x sin of the angle, 1.077, the smallest scale that fills the page again, and AddToPowerClip into a page-size rectangle crops it. The colour bars and the grey ramp at the bottom are level again. Converging verticals (perspective) are not corrected: the dialog's perspective handles have no object-model equivalent.
script ran

verified.note: The 2.5 degree input tilt is removed: the bar row is level in the result (slope -0.06 degrees, 0.3 px residual) with no empty wedges, and sharpness matches a plain bicubic rotate-and-scale of the input. Converging verticals are not corrected (no route), and the 1.077 crop cuts off the plate's bottom type row.

manual_steps: Photoshop: crop the empty wedges with the Crop Tool (Document.crop(bounds, angle) by script), or select them and run Edit > Content-Aware Fill.
Several planes (a building corner): Edit > Perspective Warp by hand (interactive only).

cards.name: Upscale for print or large display
cards.summary: Enlarges a small photo to print or banner size with detail-preserving resampling, then cleans and sharpens the result.
use_for: web-resolution images that must go to print
old small photos for a poster or banner
crops that need more pixels
avoid: expecting real detail from a tiny source: 2x is safe, beyond 3-4x faces and type look invented or mushy
upscaling a noisy or JPEG-damaged image: clean it first (denoise / JPEG artefact recipes)
AI and generative upscalers invent detail: not for news or evidence photos
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Script (new first step): Image > Image Size to 1280 px wide (bicubic sharper), a stand-in for a small source photo; the recipe starts from one, and the test photo is 1920 px. Ran.

Image > Image Size (script: resizeImage): 3840 px wide with the height in proportion (3.0 times the 1280 px source, 3840 x 2160), Preserve Details resampling (the script API has no Preserve Details 2.0 member; choose 2.0 in the dialog by hand). The settings-free route carries the probe's 200 px and bicubic, so the size and method come from the script. Ran.
Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object: ran (the label 'photo' now names the converted Layer 0), so the filters that follow are smart filters.
Filter > Blur > Surface Blur, Radius 2, Threshold 8: ran, very light.

Filter > Sharpen > Smart Sharpen at the new size: Amount 120 %, Radius 1.2 px, Remove Lens Blur. Ran; the document ends at 3840 x 2160 px, and the 1:1 crop is 1024 x 1024 px of the lower-right region. Measured on that crop against the 1920 px original enlarged to the same size: a plain bicubic enlargement of the 1280 px source has a Laplacian detail of 68, the plan's result 199 (the reference is 291), and the mean absolute error against the reference is 2.7 levels for bicubic and 2.4 for the plan. The 1:1 crop shows smooth, clean edges: the colour-bar boundary and hairline target are sharp with no stair-steps or blocking; a faint 1 px overshoot shows along the bar edges; the foreground texture is soft, as expected at 3 times. Untested: AI or Generative Upscale and Camera Raw Super Resolution (credits or no script route, manual).

steps.note: Setup (script): Bitmap.Resample(480, 270) shrinks the photo to a small source, the starting point of an upscale. (Resample keeps the resolution, so the object shrinks on the page; the next step brings it back.)

steps.script:
s.Bitmap.Resample(960, 540, True)
s.SetSize(PW, PH)
s.SetPosition(0.0, PH)
result = s
steps.note: First doubling: Bitmap.Resample(960, 540) with anti-aliasing (the call has no machine-learning mode, so this is ordinary resampling), and the object is set back to the page size.
Unsharp Mask after the first doubling: 160 percent, radius 3, threshold 3: restores the edge contrast the resampling softened before the second doubling.

steps.script:
s.Bitmap.Resample(1920, 1080, True)
s.SetSize(PW, PH)
s.SetPosition(0.0, PH)
result = s
steps.note: Second doubling: Bitmap.Resample(1920, 1080), the 4x enlargement done in two 2x steps (the recipe's safe route). Still ordinary resampling: no detail is invented.
Final Unsharp Mask: 160 percent, radius 4, threshold 3, after the enlargement: the edges are crisp again (radius 1 changed nothing visible in the first run).
script ran

ApplyBitmapEffect('UnsharpMaskEffect Percentage=160,Radius=4,Threshold=3')

manual_steps: Bigger jumps: Image > Generative Upscale (credits, no script route) or Camera Raw's Super Resolution (2x, by hand).

cards.name: Dehaze a washed-out photo
cards.summary: Cuts haze, smog or a foggy window look: deeper contrast and colour in the washed-out areas, a little midtone clarity.
use_for: landscape and city photos shot through haze or smog
photos taken through glass
flat, low-contrast drone shots
faded scans
avoid: strong Dehaze on skies: banding and dark corners; keep it under 50 and mask the sky if needed
photos that are meant to look atmospheric
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

cards.name: Fix lens faults: colour fringes, vignetting, distortion
cards.summary: Removes the camera lens's colour fringes along high-contrast edges, brightens dark corners and straightens barrel distortion with manual Lens Correction sliders.
use_for: wide-angle architecture and interior photos
product shots on white with fringed edges
cheap-lens and phone photos with dark corners
avoid: photos with lens metadata: the automatic profile corrections in Camera Raw are better and need no slider guessing
creative vignettes you want to keep
CorelDRAW: lens distortion lives in Bitmaps > Straighten Image (dialog only, see the straighten recipe)
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

cards.name: Clean JPEG compression artefacts
cards.summary: Softens the blocky 8x8 tiles, edge ringing and smeared colour of an over-compressed JPEG before it is reused, enlarged or printed.
use_for: images saved from chat apps and social platforms
low-quality stock or client-supplied JPEGs
web images that must go to print
avoid: re-saving as JPEG at low quality afterwards: the artefacts come straight back; save PNG or high-quality JPEG
expecting lost detail to return: it smooths damage, it does not rebuild texture
Illustrator: no pixel retouching; retouch in Photoshop (or CorelDRAW for simple fixes) and place the result.

steps.note: Layer > Smart Objects > Convert to Smart Object: ran (the label 'photo' now names the converted Layer 0), so the filters that follow are smart filters. The plan's input is the test photo re-saved as a JPEG at quality 10, so it carries 8 x 8 blocking and ringing, the damage this recipe repairs.
Filter > Noise > Reduce Noise: Reduce Color Noise 30 %, Sharpen Details 0 %, Remove JPEG Artifact on. Ran. Keep Reduce Color Noise moderate, as colour bleeds across hard borders at 100 %.

Filter > Blur > Surface Blur, Radius 4, Threshold 18 (3 / 12 in the first run, on a photo with no blocks): ran. Measured at 1:1 on the lower-right 512 x 512 px: the ratio of the brightness step across 8-px block boundaries to the step inside blocks is 1.36 for the damaged input and 0.94 after the two filters (1.22 for the clean photo), and over the photo area at 960 px the mean absolute error against the clean photo falls from 4.5 to 4.0 levels. The flat colour bars stay clean, but the hairline target is smeared (its error against the clean photo rises from about 10 to 19 levels) and the grey ramp keeps its stepped bands and fine texture is a little softer (the 1:1 crop's error is slightly higher, 6.3 against 5.6, because of the softened hairlines). Radius 7 / Threshold 28 smoothed less of the blocking. Untested: a more heavily compressed JPEG, and saving as PNG or high-quality JPEG afterwards.
